title: Jeremiah 8:14–22
context: Several voices speak in this unit. In 8:14–16 the people speak, calling one another into the fortified cities and confessing that “we have sinned against the LORD” as the enemy’s horses are heard from Dan. In 8:17 the LORD speaks of serpents that cannot be charmed. Then a voice of grief follows (8:18–22). It is often heard as Jeremiah’s, though some hear the LORD’s own sorrow; the WEB marks within it the people’s cry, “Isn’t the LORD in Zion?”, the LORD’s answering question about their idols (8:19), and the people’s lament, “The harvest is past. The summer has ended, and we are not saved” (8:20). The unit closes with “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there?” (8:22). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: judgment is announced with grief, not indifference, and the people’s wound is real.

verses.text: “Why do we sit still? Assemble yourselves! Let’s enter into the fortified cities, and let’s be silent there; for the LORD our God has put us to silence, and given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The people say, “Why do we sit still?… we have sinned against the LORD.” Arminian readers note the late confession. The people recognize their sin only as disaster approaches and flee to the fortified cities.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear an admission of guilt under the pressure of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the people’s own voice, confessing sin and despairing of escape, and neither reads more into the confession than the text gives.

verses.text: We looked for peace, but no good came; and for a time of healing, and behold, dismay!
verses.arminianNotes: “We looked for peace, but no good came.” Arminian readers note the echo of the false prophets’ “Peace, peace” (8:11). The peace they were promised has not come, and the people are left in dismay.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the failure of false hope. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the reassurance of false leaders could not withstand reality, and both see it as the people’s honest lament.

verses.text: The snorting of his horses is heard from Dan. The whole land trembles at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones; for they have come, and have devoured the land and all that is in it, the city and those who dwell therein.”
verses.arminianNotes: The snorting of the enemy’s horses is heard from Dan. Arminian readers note that Dan lay in the far north, so the invasion is heard from the edge of the land. The whole land trembles at the approach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as describing the advancing enemy from the north. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry of approaching judgment, and neither presses identifications beyond what the text says.

verses.text: “For, behold, I will send serpents, adders among you, which will not be charmed; and they will bite you,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will send serpents… which will not be charmed.” Arminian readers note the image of a danger that cannot be warded off. No technique or trick will turn aside this judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of judgment that cannot be escaped by human means. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a vivid picture of the LORD’s judgment, and neither builds a wider point on the image beyond what the text states.

verses.text: Oh that I could comfort myself against sorrow! My heart is faint within me.
verses.arminianNotes: “Oh that I could comfort myself against sorrow! My heart is faint within me.” Arminian readers often hear Jeremiah’s own grief. The prophet who announces judgment does so with a breaking heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear deep sorrow, often taken as Jeremiah’s, though some hear the LORD’s grief. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that judgment is announced with anguish, not indifference, and both hold the speaker’s identity with care.

verses.text: Behold, the voice of the cry of the daughter of my people from a land that is very far off: “Isn’t the LORD in Zion? Isn’t her King in her?” “Why have they provoked me to anger with their engraved images, and with foreign idols?”
verses.arminianNotes: The people cry, “Isn’t the LORD in Zion?” and the LORD answers with a question about their idols. Arminian readers note the people’s confusion: they assume God’s presence guarantees safety, as in the temple slogan (7:4).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people’s question answered by God’s charge of idolatry. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as revealing why the expected help has not come, and both note its link with the false security of 7:4.

verses.text: “The harvest is past. The summer has ended, and we are not saved.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The harvest is past. The summer has ended, and we are not saved.” Arminian readers hear the lament of missed opportunity. The seasons when deliverance might have come have passed without rescue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the people’s despair at a rescue that has not come. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an honest and poignant lament, and both apply it with care as a call to respond to God while there is opportunity.

verses.text: For the hurt of the daughter of my people, I am hurt. I mourn. Dismay has taken hold of me.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the hurt of the daughter of my people, I am hurt.” Arminian readers note the speaker’s identification with the suffering people. Grief over judgment is shared, not observed from a distance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear compassion for the wounded people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the speaker mourns with those under judgment, and both see in it a model for compassionate response to the suffering of others.

verses.text: Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then isn’t the health of the daughter of my people recovered?
verses.arminianNotes: “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there?” Arminian readers note the question about healing. Gilead was associated with balm (compare Genesis 37:25), yet the people’s health has not been restored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a lament about a wound that remains unhealed. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as given, an anguished question about healing, and neither forces it into a fuller doctrine than the text itself states.
